wa_mount_torment_torment_forbidden_trave.rappel_count_note: Ten rappels in all on a single rope brings you from Forbidden's summit back to the base of the cat scratch gully - roughly three down the West Ridge crest to the notch, then the rest down the gully system. That total is the traverse's own route description and matches independent trip reports (one party logged 'several' to regain the notch and then six more to the glacier remnants). Two ropes roughly halves it; five or six single-rope rappels are described for the rock rib below the notch alone. Per-rappel lengths are not published anywhere for this descent - the stored figures are estimates, not measurements.

wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.rappels: 7-10 rappels (mix of double- and single-rope, 60m ropes) back down the ridge to the bivy col, interspersed with downclimbing; existing slings/rap rings are present at most stations but should be inspected or backed up
wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb roughly 30 ft off the north side of the notch to easier rock, then reverse the ridge via a long string of rappels (double-rope where two ropes are carried) interspersed with downclimbing — accounts report anywhere from about 7 to 10 rappels total, including a double-rope rappel off the crux crack pitch — back down to the bivy col. Existing slings and rap rings are present at most stations but the rock is loose, so back up or replace suspect anchors. From the col, reverse the approach gully and climbers' path back around Thornton Lake and out the Thornton Lakes Trail to the trailhead. On a late-September descent the third rappel used nearly all of a 60 m rope (a 57 m rope fell short), and some of the older anchors needed to be cut away and replaced; carry spare cord and full-length ropes.

wa_mount_triumph_west_route.rappels: A long series of rappels (double- and single-rope) reversing the southeast ramp and west-side benches back down
wa_mount_triumph_west_route.rappel_count_note: The descent reverses the southeast ramp and west-side benches with a long series of double- and single-rope rappels. No count or station list is published, so none is given; carry two ropes and spare cord.

wa_mount_washington_olympic_winter_direc.rappels: Full double-rope (2x60m) rappels down snow slopes on descent
wa_mount_washington_olympic_winter_direc.descent_text: The winter descent is long and largely on snow; carry two 60m ropes to allow full-length double-rope rappels down the steepest slopes, supplemented by face-in downclimbing on lower-angle sections. In late February the steep, hard snow below the summit ridge called for a pair of rope rappels, using trees or snow anchors, before the angle eased.

rappel_detail.pull: Double ropes the whole way. Rappelling this way works, but stuck ropes are a known risk; pull steadily.
rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 1 of about 10, on double ropes, off the summit block toward the north arete and the rock trough at the head of the couloir.
hazards: There is nothing fixed to inspect here — the anchor is whatever you can build out of what is stacked on the summit
rappel_detail.station: Comes straight off the summit block, rigged around a stack of blocks rather than any fixed gear.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 2 of about 10, into the upper couloir. Where the flanking rock gives out, at least one party rappelled off a buried deadman picket.
hazards: This face sheds rock steadily and the couloir is the funnel it all comes down — anchoring on the flanking wall keeps you and the ropes out of the middle of it
rappel_detail.station: Into the upper couloir. The anchors are on the rock walls flanking the couloir rather than in the ice — that is where the first ascent placed pins on the way down, and where later parties still rig. Where the flanking rock gives out, at least one party rappelled off a buried picket.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 3 of about 10, down the north-side couloir on double ropes.
rappel_detail.anchor: slung horn, pin or gear anchor on the flanking rock wall
rappel_detail.station: On the rock wall flanking the couloir, not in the ice: that is where the first ascent placed pins on the way down and where later parties still rig. Expect to build or back up the anchor with slings on horns or your own gear rather than trusting old fixed pins.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 4 of about 10, down the north-side couloir on double ropes.
rappel_detail.anchor: slung horn, pin or gear anchor on the flanking rock wall
hazards: The couloir funnels everything that comes off the face. Keep the party and the ropes against the flanking wall, out of the middle.
rappel_detail.station: On the rock wall flanking the couloir, not in the ice: that is where the first ascent placed pins on the way down and where later parties still rig. Expect to build or back up the anchor with slings on horns or your own gear rather than trusting old fixed pins.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 5 of about 10, down the north-side couloir on double ropes.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 6 of about 10, down the north-side couloir on double ropes.
rappel_detail.anchor: slung horn, pin or gear anchor on the flanking rock wall
hazards: Double-rope pulls can snag on the rock walls of the couloir; pull steadily and watch the knot clear each edge.
rappel_detail.station: On the rock wall flanking the couloir, not in the ice: that is where the first ascent placed pins on the way down and where later parties still rig. Expect to build or back up the anchor with slings on horns or your own gear rather than trusting old fixed pins.

rappel_detail.anchor: slung horn, pin or gear anchor on the flanking rock wall

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel 10 of about 10, reaching the snow and the bergschrund at the foot of the couloir. Parties often stop rappelling earlier and downclimb the lower couloir when the snow allows.
hazards: The bergschrund at the foot of the north-face couloir still has to be crossed to reach the glacier, and it is the last thing you deal with after a long technical descent
rappel_detail.station: The rappels do not necessarily reach the bottom. Parties commonly stop rappelling partway and downclimb the rest of the couloir, frequently in the dark.

wa_nooksack_tower_beckey_route.rappels: About 10 double-rope rappels down the north-side couloir back to the bergschrund, anchored on the rock walls flanking the couloir; sometimes more, or fewer where the lower couloir can be downclimbed.
wa_nooksack_tower_beckey_route.rappel_count_note: About ten double-rope rappels from the summit to the glacier, with anchors built on the rock walls flanking the couloir. Parties describe ten or more; the count drops when the lower couloir is in condition to downclimb. Rappel lengths are not published station by station.

wa_nooksack_tower_south_face.rappel_count_note: The one first-hand account of this descent records four rappels on two 60 m ropes, ending at the col rather than continuing to the glacier, with one station off a fixed titanium knifeblade equalised with a stopper. Other reports vary from four to ten or more depending on the line taken and how much snow is on it. No per-station distance is published and no station positions are documented, so plan to find or build anchors rather than to work down a fixed list.

rappel_detail.notes: First of three single-rope rappels down the south side toward the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire.
hazards: Rope drag and route-finding after the slab traverse make this a confusing place to arrive; the anchor is above where most parties stop
The descent is repeatedly described as windy, which throws a tossed rope off line
rappel_detail.station: About 30 m down from where the route tops out and on the skier's right, not on the summit itself. The top station is a bolted anchor - reached, from the West Face finish, by continuing about 50 ft above the top of that route's last pitch. It is worth noting where this anchor is on the way up: parties descending at dusk say knowing where the first anchors are is what makes a late descent reasonable. First of three single-rope rappels heading down toward the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire.

rappel_detail.notes: Second single-rope rappel continuing toward the notch/gully.
hazards: This is the rappel reported as coming up about 5 ft short on a 60 m rope, finished with a short downclimb. Expect it rather than discovering it at the ends
The gully is loose and chossy, and snow-covered well into the season
rappel_detail.station: Second of the three single-rope rappels, down into the gully.

rappel_detail.notes: Third single-rope rappel reaching the notch.
hazards: The gully here is the one parties mistakenly ascend when route-finding up the chasm; on the way down it is loose and often snow-filled
Rockfall onto anyone still on the rappel above
rappel_detail.station: Third single-rope rappel, landing in the notch between North and South Early Winters Spire - often snow-covered. There is a tree at the notch that parties use as the landmark for the anchors here. A few minutes of class-3 scrambling and downclimbing links this to the chockstone station.

rappel_detail.notes: Largely free-hanging double-rope rappel past the giant chockstone (~50 ft of air) from bolts on top of the chockstone.
rappel_detail.anchor: bolted anchor on top of the chockstone
hazards: Fully free-hanging with no way to reach rock once you are on it
You arrive at this station from above by scrambling loose gully ground, which is where material gets knocked onto anyone below
rappel_detail.station: The rappel this descent is known for. Below the notch, a short scramble leads to the giant chockstone in the gully; the station is a bolted rap anchor on top of the chockstone - not tat, and the same bolts parties belay from on the way up when climbing the Chockstone Route. The rappel goes off the chockstone and hangs completely free for around 50 ft, and is routinely described as the longest free-hanging rappel the party has done.

rappel_detail.notes: Final short (~30 ft) rappel, or downclimb/scramble alternative, back to the base.
hazards: Loose, steep gully walking either way
rappel_detail.station: A few more minutes of class-3 scrambling and downclimbing below the chockstone, then a last short rappel of about 30 ft off a tree to the ground. Some parties downclimb this instead of rigging it.

wa_labor_pains.rappels: Many parties now descend a separate bolted rappel line down the West Face, which runs between the West Face route and Labor Pains itself, instead of the Chockstone Route stations. The Chockstone line is the original chockstone/notch descent down the south side: three single-rope rappels to the notch, a largely free-hanging double-rope rappel past the giant chockstone, and a short rappel off a tree to the ground. Its second gully rappel comes up about 5 ft short on a 60 m rope and is finished with a downclimb.
wa_labor_pains.rappel_count_note: These five stations are the original chockstone/notch descent down the south side, and the count assumes a single rope for the three upper rappels plus two ropes for the chockstone rappel - accounts describe it as up to five rappels depending on conditions and the number of ropes carried, and parties with two ropes throughout combine some of the upper ones. The second gully rappel comes up about 5 ft short on a 60 m. Important: many Labor Pains parties now use a different descent. A separate bolted rappel line was established down the West Face, running between the West Face route and Labor Pains itself, and it is that West Face line, rather than anything in this route's own gear list, that wants a 70 m rope; the list here is a 60 m. That line shares only the first anchor with the chockstone descent - from it you head down the West Face instead of into the gully - and has nothing else in common with the stations listed here. It is currently six stations on bolts and chains ending a minute from the base of the routes, with one rappel that a 60 m does not make (parties report needing to block and extend a strand, or carry a 70), and a last anchor that is genuinely hard to find, on a rib below some shrubs and skier's left as you walk down loose dirt from the fifth station. Some parties still rappel from a nearby dead tree carrying no slings, which is not the anchor. Do not blend the two lines: the station list shown is the chockstone line.
